hints: Look carefully at the three curves. Decreasing carbon dioxide means going from Z (7.0 kPa) down to X (3.0 kPa). Which way does the curve move, left or right?
Remember what a left shift means for affinity. Higher percentage saturation at the same oxygen partial pressure means haemoglobin holds onto oxygen more tightly.
walkthrough:
**Spot what decreasing carbon dioxide does on the graph**

Decreasing means high to low, so move from Z at $7.0\text{ kPa}$ to X at $3.0\text{ kPa}$. You can see curve X sits to the left of and above curve Z.

At any same partial pressure of oxygen, X shows a higher percentage saturation.

**Link the shift to the Bohr effect**

A shift to the left means higher affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen. This is the Bohr effect in reverse: less $CO_2$, less $H^+$ from carbonic acid, higher pH, so haemoglobin holds oxygen more strongly.

**Decide on loading versus unloading**

Higher affinity is great for taking up (loading) oxygen in the lungs, because haemoglobin becomes saturated more easily. But it is poor for releasing (unloading) oxygen in tissues, because haemoglobin is reluctant to let go.

So decreasing $pCO_2$ gives more efficient uptake but less efficient release.

options.A: Uptake is not less efficient. The left shift to X shows higher saturation at the same oxygen pressure, so loading is improved.
options.B: This is backwards. Decreasing carbon dioxide increases affinity, so uptake improves and release becomes harder, not the other way round.
options.C: Correct. The left shift to X means higher affinity, so haemoglobin loads oxygen more easily but holds it too tightly to release it easily.
options.D: Release is not more efficient. Higher affinity means haemoglobin keeps oxygen, so unloading at respiring tissues is reduced.
